schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note this fourth speech lacks the usual 'Elihu answered,' being introduced only as a continuation 'in honour of the number three'; Ellicott finds it hard to acquit Elihu of the very arrogance he ascribed to Job.
Henry hears Elihu begging patience and pleading his warrant — he speaks 'on God's behalf' as an advocate, though a man may pretend to speak for God who really speaks for himself.
Gill renders 'added': Elihu paused to see whether Job would reply, and, having more to deliver, went on.
Clarke gives Heath's outline of the whole chapter — Elihu vindicating God's impartial justice, his promises and threats, and the closing proofs from nature.

outliers.note: Charges that Elihu's great professions of zeal for God are not all warranted, and that he is not free of the arrogance he condemns in Job.

themes: the honest advocate versus the self-important speaker

schools.summary: Gill notes the word 'suffer me' has the signification of a crown, taken with Aben Ezra as 'do me the honour of thy presence a little longer,' not 'stand about me.'

Keil and Delitzsch set out the strophe and its rare, borrowed diction — the Aramaic katter, a poetic Aramaism, a diminutive from the popular speech — the sense being 'there still are words in favour of Eloah.'
Henry reads a plea for a patient hearing, Elihu's warrant lying in the nobility of his theme, for more may always be spoken on God's behalf.
Clarke keeps it plain: 'I have other proofs to allege in behalf of God's justice and providence.'

themes: words still to be said for Eloah

schools.summary: Gill offers three senses of 'from afar' — former ages and foreign lands, God himself on high, or 'knowledge concerning him that is afar off,' God.
Clarke reads 'from afar' as remote antiquity and heaven, pointing to the chapter's closing proofs; Wesley widens the brief to God's works of creation and providence in all ages and places.

Ellicott dryly asks whether this is not just what Bildad had said (ch. 8:8), and whether Elihu's teaching in v.6 is really different; Keil and Delitzsch complete the vow, 'to my Creator will I ascribe right.'

outliers.note: Suggests Elihu's grand preface promises more novelty than it delivers, echoing Bildad's appeal to the former age.

themes: I will fetch my knowledge from afar
the whole theatre of nature and history

schools.summary: Gill takes 'my words shall not be false' at plain worth — truth spoken briefly and clearly on the weighty subject of God's righteousness.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'one perfect in knowledge stands before thee' and take it of Elihu himself; Ellicott lays bare the ambiguity, noting the AV looks as though he meant himself (so too the Vulgate, cf. ch. 37:16).
Clarke turns 'with thee' into a compliment to Job, the well-informed judge; Wesley refers it to God, 'a God of perfect knowledge, by whom all thy words and actions are weighed.'

debates.question: Who is 'he that is perfect in knowledge'?

sides.position: God, whose omniscience weighs every word
Job himself, competent to judge the argument
Elihu himself, vouching for his own sufficiency (the plain look of the AV)

themes: my words shall not be false
perfect in knowledge — God, Job, or Elihu
confidence in God or in the man

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the 'behold' and the might it announces — the Almighty seen in creation, providence, and redemption.
Henry seizes the wonder that infinite might 'despises not any': God stoops to notice the meanest, a reason we should honour all men, his grace no diminution to him.

Clarke prefers the active 'he despiseth not any' (reproaches no man for want of knowledge) over the passive, and reads 'mighty in strength of heart'; Wesley: his greatness makes him not despise the meanest, his strength guided by wisdom.

outliers.note: Prefers 'he despiseth not any' (God reproaches no man for lack of knowledge) to the passive rendering 'he will not be despised.'

themes: God is mighty and despiseth not any
might that stoops to the meanest

schools.summary: Gill guards 'preserveth not the life of the wicked' — God keeps them only in common providence, not the special care he shows the righteous, nor to any great length.
Keil and Delitzsch anchor the strophe, insisting the subject of the following verses is the righteous, not the wicked, comparing Psalm 107 throughout.
Clarke: God gives not life to the wicked but justice to the humble; Wesley hears a promise — 'he will in his time deliver his oppressed ones.'
Henry portrays the righteous Governor: no special care for the wicked (a reservation for the day of wrath), but right given to the poor and their quarrel avenged.

themes: he preserveth not the life of the wicked
the righteous, not the wicked, in view

schools.summary: Gill multiplies the senses of the unwithdrawn eye — providence, love, and mercy from everlasting, never separated from the love of God.
Ellicott takes 'the righteous' as the righteous man in the singular, comparing the God who dwells on high yet beholds the lowly (Ps. 113:5-8).

Clarke repairs the second clause — 'with kings upon the throne shall he place them,' reading 'to victory' for 'for ever' (cf. Rev. 3:21); Wesley: the righteous continue exalted, not cast down like the wicked.
Henry weighs the honour and its rarity, lifting the promise to the exaltation of the righteous when their Redeemer stands at the latter day.

themes: he withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous
exalted to victory or for ever
the crown of the world to come

schools.summary: Gill insists, against the Targum, that the bound are the righteous, the fetters figurative of chastening afflictions, set here to obviate the objection that the afflicted cannot be loved.
Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the literal 'chains' from the figurative 'bands,' the pairing of Psalm 107:10.
Clarke: the fetters are means of correction, not punishment; Wesley reads the vicissitude that brings men even from a throne to a prison.
Henry widens the picture to every trouble — prison like Joseph's, sickness, poverty — Job's own case, caught in the cords of anguish.

themes: bound in fetters and cords of affliction
the righteous, not the wicked, in chains

schools.summary: Gill reads 'their work' as sins of omission or commission, held up to view in the glass of affliction.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'that they have been vainglorious,' the sin exposed a species of pride; Ellicott names Elihu's special doctrine — chastisement as discipline to reform the future, not chastise the past.
Clarke traces 'exceeded' to 'they have strengthened themselves' and trusted not the living God; Wesley: they have greatly sinned by abusing power and prosperity, as even good men are prone.
Henry: the first end of affliction is to discover past sins, showing the fact, fault, and sinfulness of sin, that they have exceeded.

themes: chastisement as discipline reforming the future

schools.summary: Gill turns over 'opens the ear to correction/instruction,' the ear first opened at conversion, and reopened when God rouses the drowsy from a whirlwind — more learned by affliction than by a sermon.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'He openeth their ear to warning,' the discipline a warning meant to be heeded.
Clarke: God gives them to understand why they are corrected, commanding them to return; Wesley: he inclines them to hearken to what he speaks by the rod.
Henry sets this among the ends of affliction — to dispose the heart to instruction (Ps. 94:12), softening the wax by grace, and to draw men off from iniquity.

themes: he openeth their ear to discipline
the command to return from iniquity
grace, not pain itself, opens the ear

schools.summary: Gill fixes 'obey and serve him' as obedience to the rod — hearing it, humbling oneself, returning from iniquity.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'if they hear and yield,' taking the verb as doing another's will; Ellicott alone lets the objection stand, that this teaching is as hard to square with fact as the friends' notions of retribution.
Clarke owns the apparent exceptions yet holds the rule true of every genuine follower of God, happy in whatever circumstances.
Henry presses the double promise — outward prosperity so far as is for God's glory and our good, and the inward pleasure of communion and peace.

outliers.note: Grants that Elihu's promise of prosperity for the obedient is no easier to reconcile with actual fact than the friends' doctrine of direct retribution.

themes: if they obey and serve him
days in prosperity and years in pleasure
the promise hard to square with fact

schools.summary: Gill sketches the man who seems righteous but kicks against the pricks, unsubmissive and murmuring.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'they pass away by the bow and expire in lack of knowledge,' the weapon a shaft.
Clarke prefers 'by a dart they shall pass by' (or 'as an arrow,' Good) — continual danger, falling before half their days — though the Vulgate keeps the sword.
Henry reads 'without knowledge' doubly — cut off unaware, or dying for want of the knowledge they had means to gain; such die without grace.

debates.question: What is the instrument of the disobedient's ruin?

sides.position: 'perish by the sword' (the AV and the Vulgate)
'pass by as an arrow / a dart' (the Hebrew shelach)

themes: if they obey not they perish

schools.summary: Gill offers both — they treasure up God's wrath against the day of wrath, or (with Jarchi) their own wrath, 'putting the nose' against God in pride.
Keil and Delitzsch decide the wrath is the man's own impatience, marking him estranged from God; Ellicott reads 'godless in heart' and 'cry not for help.'
Clarke insists the word means the profligate and impious, not the form-without-power hypocrite, and 'not the meaning in Job'; Wesley: they cry not to God when he binds them.
Henry draws the doctrine of hypocrisy — it lies in the heart, and its mischief is to heap up wrath against the great day (Rom. 2:5).

sides.position: God's wrath, treasured against the impenitent
the man's own impatience and wrath against God

debates.question: Are these 'hypocrites' or the openly profane?

sides.position: hypocrites in heart, form without power
the godless or profane, having neither form nor power

themes: the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath
they cry not when he bindeth them

schools.summary: Gill reads 'die in youth' as premature death, the word an 'excussion' (Vulgate 'in a tempest'), Jarchi 'by strangling.'
Keil and Delitzsch render 'their soul dieth in the vigour of youth, and their life is like that of the unclean.'

Clarke fixes the qedeshim — the temple-prostitutes of Baal and Ashtoreth, Venus and Priapus (Good, 'the rabble'; LXX, 'wounded by the angels'); Wesley reads Sodomites, then the unclean spirits after death.
Henry reads the sudden death and the second death, the life after death among the unclean spirits barred from the holy city.

debates.question: Who are 'the unclean' among whom they live?

sides.position: the qedeshim, cult-prostitutes and vile company in this life
the unclean spirits, the devil and his angels, after death

themes: the qedeshim or the unclean spirits
the brief life and the long death

schools.summary: Gill holds the 'in' fast: not a rescue out of affliction but a deliverance within it, God upholding and comforting the godly poor.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read rather that God 'delivereth the afflicted by his affliction,' the trouble itself the means, 'and openeth their ear by oppression.'
Clarke suggests the verb may mean 'he shall make them exult, or sing for joy, in oppression,' like the three Hebrews in the furnace; Wesley: God causeth them to hear and do his will.
Henry turns the comfort on Job: God opens the ear of the broken and contrite and speaks good words even before he delivers.

debates.question: Does God deliver the poor 'in' affliction or 'by' it?

sides.position: delivered IN affliction — upheld and comforted within it
delivered BY affliction — the trouble itself the means of rescue

themes: he delivereth the poor in his affliction

schools.summary: Gill takes it conditionally: had Job hearkened and submitted, thus it would have been with him.
Clarke: had he obeyed, his state would be widely different; Wesley: he would have been brought into ease and freedom.
Henry spells the double blessing — enlarged into a broad place, and enriched with a table of fatness (Deut. 32:14).

Ellicott reads it not conditionally but indicatively — 'he hath removed thee from the mouth of an adversary' — God's mercy already begun, spoiled by Job's daring; Keil and Delitzsch render 'out of the jaws of distress to a broad place' and take it as the transition to the reproach.

sides.position: conditional — what God WOULD have done had Job submitted
indicative — what God HAS actually done, a mercy Job spoiled

themes: the doctrine brought home to Job

schools.summary: Gill offers two constructions and leans to the graver — not that Job lived a wicked life, but that in his impatience he does as the wicked do.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'thou art become full of the judging of the evil-doer: judging and judgment lay hold on one another.'

Clarke: acting like the wicked, Job is dealt with as they are — adding that the friends knew nothing of Satan's permission; Wesley: Job has justified the hard speeches of the wicked and maintained their cause.
Henry: Job stands in his own light, the cause of his own trouble, and judgment takes hold as on any who keeps such company (Bishop Patrick).

outliers.note: Observes that none of Job's friends, Elihu included, knew of the permission God had given Satan to afflict an innocent man — so their whole charge is built on ignorance.

themes: thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked
the fault in temper not in life
the friends' ignorance of the real cause

schools.summary: Gill weighs wrath in Job (his impatience) or wrath in God (vindictive justice), the afflictions of the godly 'a little wrath,' love displeased.
Clarke: a time when God punishes the wicked — redeem the time; Wesley: wrath conceived against Job, and no ransom then accepted.
Henry: a friendly caution not to make light of divine vengeance; even good men are kept to duty by the fear of God's wrath.

Keil and Delitzsch break with the line entirely — 'let not anger entice thee to scorning, and let not the greatness of the ransom mislead thee'; Ellicott keeps nearer the AV but notes the literal 'let not a great ransom deliver thee.'

sides.position: that no ransom can deliver once wrath has seized a man
that Job must not let anger entice him to scorning, nor imagine a great ransom could buy him off

outliers.note: Read the couplet against the whole tradition: a warning that anger not seduce Job to mockery, and that the greatness of the ransom not mislead him — not that no ransom can deliver.

themes: the great ransom that cannot deliver

schools.summary: Gill reads riches, of no weight with God (Broughton, 'thy nobleness'); neither gold nor a fortress can bribe or bar him.
Wesley keeps the sense — all Job's riches and strongest forces would be nothing.
Ellicott confesses the words doubtful ('will he esteem thy riches?' or 'will thy cry avail?'); Keil and Delitzsch decide for the cry — 'shall thy crying place thee beyond distress?'
Henry: no escaping wrath by money or by rescue, for God's justice cannot be bribed and none can deliver out of his hand (Prov. 11:4).

debates.question: Does the verse deny that riches, or that crying, can save?

sides.position: riches, gold, and force cannot deliver
Job's crying and effort cannot place him beyond distress

themes: nor gold nor forces of strength
riches or the cry for help

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses of 'the night' but settles, most likely, on the night of death Job had so often wished.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the philology — 'pant not after the night' that removes peoples fixed in their place — and draw the argument from nations to the individual; Ellicott agrees it is death, and reads 'peoples,' nations.
Wesley makes it sharp: the night of death would leave Job irrecoverably gone; let him take heed lest God grant his wish in anger.
Henry reads the last false refuge — no absconding by night, for darkness hides not from God (Ps. 139:11-12); wrath pursues some into that night.

themes: peoples cut off in their place

schools.summary: Gill takes 'regard not iniquity' of Job's impatience and murmuring, or of the evil of desiring the night of death.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'incline not to evil, for this thou hast chosen rather than affliction' — a deliberate preference for contending over enduring.
Clarke: to long for death is an insult to providence, preferring death to affliction and one's own wisdom to God's; Wesley: Job has chosen to quarrel with God rather than submit.
Henry generalizes: never think a favourable thought of sin, for there is more evil in the least sin than in the greatest affliction.

themes: the poison preferred to the cure

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the lift into the hymn of God's majesty, the gathering storm suggesting the imagery (cf. ch. 38:1); Keil and Delitzsch defend 'teacher' over the LXX's 'sovereign/lord,' since the word has no link to the term for lord and Elihu loves to make God a teacher.
Gill hears God exalting himself above all creaturely praise, and exalting his Son and his people.
Clarke turns it on Job — he has brought thee low but can raise thee, and who can teach like him?; Wesley: presume not to teach him who teaches by the Bible and by his Son.

debates.question: Is God here 'a teacher like him' or 'a ruler/lord like him'?

sides.position: teacher — the sense of the Targum, Syriac, and Jerome
lord or ruler — the Septuagint's 'sovereign,' followed by many moderns
holders: Septuagint (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

themes: the speech lifts into the hymn of majesty

schools.summary: Gill: God prescribes men's paths but none can prescribe his, nor tell him whom to afflict or how long, nor call him to account.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'who hath appointed him his way, and who dare say, Thou doest iniquity?'
Clarke: has God taken instructions from any man? and who can prove one unrighteous or unwise act in all creation?
Henry gathers it into three — absolute sovereign, incomparable teacher, unexceptionably just — weighing 'who CAN say' (with cause and proof), for the King of kings can do no wrong.

themes: who hath enjoined him his way
who can say Thou hast wrought iniquity
the flawless justice none can impeach

schools.summary: Henry makes the verse the ground of submission: God's whole work is illustrious, plain to every eye, to be magnified as glorious (Rom. 1:20; Ps. 19:3).
Gill hears both creation-providence and the chastisement of God's people — magnified when borne patiently.
Clarke bids Job survey the operation of God's hands instead of fretting; Wesley: magnify every work and condemn none.
Ellicott notes the rival 'whereof men sing' but prefers 'which men behold'; Keil and Delitzsch in fact render 'which men have sung.'

debates.question: Does the last clause read 'which men behold' or 'whereof men sing'?

sides.position: 'which men behold' — suiting the context best
'whereof men have sung'

themes: remember that thou magnify his work
the visible work as ground of submission

schools.summary: Gill: the work is seen not only by the wise but by the common people, whether creation or God's afflictive providences.

Clarke: he who sees no infinite skill in earth and heaven is ignorant or lying against conscience; Wesley: all who are not stupid must see it, and it may be seen from afar, whence Elihu passes to particular instances.
Henry: the work is plain to every man, even without revelation, the heavens and earth declaring Omnipotence.

themes: the hinge from doctrine to demonstration
led out of doors to the clouds

schools.summary: Gill unfolds the greatness (and, on one reading, the 'much/many' of the divine persons), but rests the weight on 'we know him not' — we know that he is, not what he is.
Clarke reduces it to three propositions — omnipotent, unsearchable, eternal — too sublime for paraphrase; Wesley: eternal in being and counsels, above short-lived men's comprehension.
Henry: God great, and therefore unknown to the bottom, a Being without beginning or period, the great 'I AM.'
Keil and Delitzsch render 'God is exalted — we know him not entirely,' noting 'unsearchable' is a later, Aramaic-tinged word.

outliers.note: Reads the word for 'great' as 'much/many' and finds in it the plurality of the divine persons, Father, Son, and Spirit.

themes: God is great and we know him not
the number of his years unsearchable

schools.summary: Gill notes Elihu opens, like Eliphaz, with rain, variously rendered 'he restrains' or 'draws up' the drops the sun exhales.
Clarke reads plain evaporation ('he exhales'), God seen in little things, the rain proportioned to its vapour; Wesley marks the wisdom of rain in drops, not spouts, a constant rotation of vapour.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the wondrous origin of rain distilling with its mist; Ellicott hears the first beginnings of the tempest, the water absorbed then distilled.
Henry adds the theology — the clouds pour down according to the vapour drawn up, every good gift from above.

themes: he maketh small the drops of water

schools.summary: Gregory the Great weighs Elihu himself — learned and arrogant, roses among thorns — as one who abandons the low ground of morality and rises to the heights of prophecy, an unworthy vessel that may receive holy words (like Saul, or Balaam's ass) without attaining a holy nature.
Gill keeps to the rain's liberality — dropped on the fields of men, gently and abundantly, though sometimes on the wilderness where no man is.
Clarke keeps the mechanism and records the Septuagint's addition — the clouds overshadowing multitudes, 'is not thy mind transported, thy heart ready to part from thy body?'
Henry draws out 'upon man' — special respect to man, the rain falling on just and unjust alike (Matt. 5:45), the river of God full of water (Ps. 65:9).

outliers.note: Reads the verse as the turn where Elihu rises from morality to prophecy, and takes him as proof that God can send true prophetic words through an unworthy, arrogant vessel, as through Saul or the speaking ass.

themes: the flawed vessel of true prophecy
gathering the fragrant from the thorns

schools.summary: Gill marvels at the cloud that begins the size of a hand and spreads to cover the heavens (1 Kings 18:44), poised and balanced as God's pavilion and man's umbrella.

Clarke: the vapour, at the mercy of every wind, is so managed that every arable land is supplied; the 'tabernacle' the firmament, the noise its tempests and thunder; Wesley keeps the two wonders of the spreading cloud and the gathered thunder.
Ellicott describes clouds heaped like mountains when the storm gathers, and renders 'the thunderings of his pavilion' (Ps. 18:11-12).
Henry draws the argument: if we cannot understand the spreading of a cloud, we cannot pretend to understand God's judicial dealings with men.

themes: the thunder that hushes the questioner

schools.summary: Gill offers several senses of 'his light' — the sun clearing the clouds (an emblem of forgiveness), the lightning, or (with Cocceius) light spread about God himself, or upon man and earth.
Clarke reads the light as lightning, the flash from the cloud, and God's control over the deep; Wesley: the lightning God's light, the cloud its candlestick, reaching to the sea's bottom.
Ellicott takes 'roots of the sea' for the clouds drawn up from the sea; Keil and Delitzsch render 'He spreadeth his light over himself,' siding with Cocceius against the AV's 'upon it.'

sides.position: upon it, the cloud, or upon man and the earth
over himself, God clothed in light

debates.question: What is 'the bottom of the sea' he covers?

sides.position: the literal deep, under God's control
the 'roots of the sea' — the clouds exhaled from it

themes: he spreadeth his light upon it
covering the roots of the sea

schools.summary: Gill catalogues the judgments by cloud — the Flood (Gen. 7:11), the Egyptian hail (Exod. 9:23), Sodom's fire (Gen. 19:24) — yet the same clouds show mercy.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'thereby he judgeth peoples, he giveth food in abundance'; Ellicott ties 'them' to the rain-clouds, judging by drought or flood, feeding by due rain.
Clarke draws the mercy at length — storms purify the air and rains fructify the earth — and rejects the rendering 'he passeth sentence amain'; Wesley keeps the balance of judgment and fatness.
Henry sums it — the produce of the clouds sometimes terror, sometimes favour, resolved into providence.

outliers.note: Rejects the proposed rendering 'he passeth sentence amain,' found in none of the versions, as losing the fine idea of the common translation.

themes: by them he judgeth the people
the cloud as scourge and storehouse
death and bread from one hand

schools.summary: Gill keeps the AV — God covers the light, the lightning hid in the cloud or the sun obscured, as in Paul's long tempest (Acts 27:20).
Wesley: thick clouds veil the sun; Clarke finds the verse 'extraordinary,' reporting the Vulgate's 'in his hands he hideth the light' and half suspecting an allusion to eclipses.
Ellicott presses the crux: the word means 'hands,' not 'clouds' — 'he covereth the lightning with his hands, and giveth it a charge that it strike the mark,' the image of a marksman hurling a bolt.

debates.question: Does God cover the sun's light with clouds, or the lightning in his hands?

sides.position: 'with clouds he covereth the light' of the sun — a veil over the sky (the AV)
'he covereth the lightning with his hands' and aims it at the mark (kaf = palm, not cloud)

themes: with clouds he covereth the light
the veiled sun or the aimed thunderbolt

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the noise' as a presage of coming rain, the sound of clouds, wind, or thunder.

Wesley: the thunder gives notice of rain, the cattle by instinct seeking shelter; Clarke offers his own bold rendering, 'its loud noise shall proclaim concerning him — a magazine of wrath against iniquity,' reading the last word as a treasury.

Keil and Delitzsch reject 'his friend' for 'his noise' — the thunder announces God; Ellicott, owning the verse 'extremely difficult,' reads 'the crash of the thunder declareth concerning him,' even the terrified cattle showing that it speaks of the God who goeth up on high.

debates.question: Does 'the noise' tell of the coming rain, or announce God himself?

sides.position: a presage of the approaching rain, which the cattle also sense
the thunder as God's voice, announcing him (reo = 'his noise,' not 'his friend')

debates.question: What is the obscure last clause?

sides.position: the cattle sensing the coming storm
the cattle terrified before the God who goeth up on high
'a magazine of wrath against iniquity' (mikneh as treasury)

outliers.note: Offers an idiosyncratic rendering, 'a magazine of wrath against iniquity,' reading the final word not as 'cattle' but as a stored-up treasury of wrath.

themes: the noise thereof sheweth concerning it
the thunder as the voice of God
the storm that heralds the whirlwind
